newsitem.title: SENEGAL: World Bank chief warns Africa on corruption.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief warns Africa on corruption.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn wrapped up a visit to Senegal on Monday with a warning to Africa to stamp out corruption.
Wolfensohn, who later left for Ghana and the second leg of a nine-day Africa tour, said that the bank would keep a watch list of anyone tainted by corruption.

"As far as World Bank projects are concerned, anyone found guilty of corruption will be put on our black list and we will not deal with them," he told a news conference at the end of a three-day visit to the West African nation.
It was a theme he touched on before leaving Washington on the tour, which also takes him to Mozambique and South Africa.
"I will be as always very frank," he said in Washington. "Corruption is one of the greatest inhibitors to investors."

Wolfensohn, who chose Africa for his first trip following his appointment in 1995, told the same U.S. news conference that African nations were making real economic progress and that he wanted to build on that success.
"Africa is the World Bank's top priority and we want to strengthen our partnerships with the region," he said. "We've got money available. What we need are satisfactory projects."
Last year the World Bank approved $2.7 billion in loans for African countries covering 53 projects.
Throughout his visit to Senegal, Wolfensohn stressed the need to open up the economy to the private sector.
"It's necessary to have confidence in the international community, to invite them here to see what the government wants in terms of investment," he said on Monday.
A Bank statement marking the end of the visit said he had expressed the Bank's commitment to support reforms and investment in energy production -- a key sector in any emerging economy.

Wolfensohn, who had talks with business leaders, had special praise for Senegal's market garden sector, which produces vegetables and fruit for export. He toured small-holdings outside the capital Dakar at the weekend.
"Personally I believe that it's possible for Senegal to be competitive without subsidising its agriculture and to compete with the North," he said.

Wolfensohn, who also had talks with Charles Konan Banny, governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO), stressed the growing importance of the West African regional market of 60 million people. The BCEAO groups most French-speaking countries in the sub-region.

Wolfensohn, who had two rounds of talks with President Abdou Diouf, paid tribute to government efforts to reform the economy. He said the private sector played an important role in Senegal and held the key to its international competitiveness.
During weekend talks with donor representatives he stressed the need for project coordination and good governance.
